17 An object travelling with a speed of 10 m s–1 has kinetic energy 1500 J.
The speed of the object is increased to 40 m s–1.
What is the new kinetic energy of the object?
A
4500 J
B
6000 J
C
24 000 J
D
1 350 000 J

hints: Compare the two speeds in $\text{m s}^{-1}$: $10$ becomes $40$, so work out the factor by which the speed increases.
Recall $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ with the same mass, so only $v^2$ changes the kinetic energy.
Square the speed factor and multiply the original $1500 \text{ J}$ by that squared factor.
walkthrough: Note the given data: $v_1 = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ with $E_{k1} = 1500 \text{ J}$, and $v_2 = 40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ for the same object so mass $m$ is unchanged.
State the governing rule: kinetic energy is $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so for constant $m$, $E_k$ is proportional to $v^2$.
Calculate the new energy: $E_{k2} = 1500 \times 16 = 24\,000 \text{ J}$, with unit $\text{J}$ as expected for energy. This is option C.

A.explanation: 4500 J assumes kinetic energy triples when speed goes from $10 \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $40 \text{m s}^{-1}$, but kinetic energy does not scale linearly with speed.

B.explanation: 6000 J assumes kinetic energy increases by the speed ratio $40/10 = 4$, but $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ depends on $v^2$ so the factor must be squared.

C.explanation: Speed increases by factor 4, so kinetic energy increases by $4^2 = 16$, giving $1500 \times 16 = 24\,000 \text{ J}$.

D.explanation: 1 350 000 J is far too large and does not follow the $v^2$ scaling from $10 \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $40 \text{m s}^{-1}$ for the same mass.
